definition: First screen of any output before use: (1) Factually correct, so do facts, figures, dates and names hold? (2) Complete, or is a relevant aspect missing? (3) Appropriate in tone and free of discriminatory claims? Review depth and additional controls follow purpose and impact.
A natural or legal person that develops an AI system, or has one developed, and places it on the market under its own name (EU AI Act Art. 3(3)).
Mechanism that computes weighted relationships between token representations and helps transformer models connect context. It establishes neither relevance nor understanding.
A contract under GDPR Art. 28 when a controller engages a processor to process personal data. Whether it is required and enough depends on the roles and the processing.
Rights of natural persons under the GDPR: access (Art. 15), rectification (Art. 16), erasure (Art. 17), restriction (Art. 18), objection (Art. 21). They apply to AI processing too.
A natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body using an AI system under its authority; personal non-professional activity is excluded (EU AI Act Art. 3(4)).
A systematic deviation that can come from data collection, labels, objectives, modeling, evaluation or deployment context. It can affect groups differently and is not automatically discrimination.
EU AI Act records kept together: AI inventory, risk classifications, training records, usage policies and incident-response protocols. It does not replace a legal review.
The field of AI that processes images and video, for example in face recognition, quality control and autonomous driving.

An assessment under GDPR Art. 35 when planned processing is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. AI can be a risk factor but does not trigger a DPIA automatically.
An example model with four protection levels for company data. The organization sets labels, criteria and permitted workflows; the level alone approves no product.
A branch of machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers to recognize patterns in complex data such as images, speech and text.
AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content that resembles real people, objects, places or events and can falsely appear authentic. The legal definition depends on the framework.
Further training of a pretrained model on selected data or preferences to adjust its behavior for particular tasks or domains. Separate evaluations show whether it worked.
AI systems that produce new content: text, images, audio, video, code. ChatGPT, DALL-E, Midjourney, Claude.
Plausible-looking output of a generative model that is unsupported, inconsistent or factually wrong. Language models do not check facts automatically.

An AI system classified as high-risk under Art. 6 in conjunction with Annex I or III. Provider duties and deployer duties differ. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force since 27 July 2026, sets 2 December 2027 for stand-alone Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for systems integrated into products.

A design in which people hold defined monitoring, intervention or decision authority. Article 14 of the EU AI Act requires effective human oversight for high-risk systems; what a human final decision looks like depends on the use case.
The process in which a trained model turns an input into an output. Every ChatGPT answer is an inference.

Skills, knowledge and understanding that allow informed AI use and awareness of opportunities, risks and possible harm (EU AI Act Art. 3(56)). Article 4 requires context-specific measures supporting the development of this literacy.
A machine-based system that turns inputs into outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations or decisions, and can work at varying levels of autonomy (EU AI Act Art. 3(1)).

The procedure that checks whether a high-risk AI system meets the requirements that apply to it. Procedure and involvement of a notified body depend on the system and legal basis; CE marking follows only where the framework provides for it.
An umbrella term for machine-based systems that derive outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations or decisions from inputs. The exact definition follows the technical or legal context.
A large model trained on extensive data that models probabilities over token sequences. Some handle modalities beyond text; product name and model version are not the same.
The field of AI in which model parameters are adjusted from data and optimization objectives. Common categories include supervised, unsupervised, self-supervised and reinforcement learning.
The trained result of a machine-learning process. It holds the learned parameters (weights) and is applied to new inputs.
The field of AI that processes natural language: translation, summarization, sentiment analysis, text generation.
A computational model of layers of connected nodes, modeled on biological neurons and the basis of deep learning.
A model fits the peculiarities or noise of its training data too closely and generalizes worse to new data. Memorization is one possible form.
Values a model adjusts during training, such as weights and bias terms. Parameter count alone compares neither quality nor cost nor suitability.
The input to a generative system, such as instruction, question, data and context. A clear prompt shapes the output and guarantees neither correctness nor quality.

A versioned collection of prompt templates for recurring tasks, with purpose, permitted inputs, example outputs, review steps and evaluation results. Benefit and limits are measured in your own process.

An attack or failure mode in which instructions inside user input or processed content push a model outside its intended behavior. OWASP lists Prompt Injection as LLM01 in its 2025 Top 10 for LLM applications.

A pattern in which a generative model receives retrieved content as context. It can improve traceability and factual accuracy. It depends on retrieval, source quality and correct use, and it prevents no hallucinations.
A course template with the fields Role, Context, Task, Format and Constraints. It makes requirements visible. Not every task needs every field, and the template guarantees no correct output.
A type of machine learning in which an agent learns by trial and error, with reward for wanted and penalty for unwanted behavior. Used in robotics and game strategies, for example.
Use of AI services or features outside the approved inventory and the intended controls, such as consumer offers, extensions, embedded features or local models.
A type of machine learning that learns the mapping from input to output from labeled examples, as in spam filters, credit scoring and image recognition.
The smallest unit an LLM processes, such as a word, part of a word or a punctuation mark. Models generate text token by token.
The data used to adjust model parameters. Selection, quality, representativeness and documentation shape behavior; model, objective, evaluation and deployment context shape it too.

A neural-network architecture presented in 2017 that uses attention and positional information. It underlies many current language models and allows highly parallel training; modern models differ in design.
A type of machine learning without labeled data in which the model finds patterns and structures itself, as in customer segmentation, anomaly detection and clustering.
